The Transcript reported that Senator John F. Kennedy was contacted to speak at Ohio Wesleyan's Political Days in the spring of 1960, but he was unable to attend due to his pre-arranged schedule [Source 1]. 

In broader coverage of the 1960 presidential race, the newspaper noted that Governor Michael DiSalle endorsed Kennedy and that Ohio's delegates were pledged as a bloc for the Massachusetts senator [Source 2]. Later that spring, the Ben Arneson Institute of Practical Politics scheduled a Democratic Day for May 16, 1960, though IPP Director Fred G. Burke explained that securing a speaker was difficult because leading Democrats were deployed to key states and non-committed Democrats were wary of visiting a state already committed to Kennedy [Source 3].

answer.text:
## Demonstrations and Rallies

Ohio Wesleyan students reacted to the Vietnam War through active participation in anti-war demonstrations, campus protests, and peace initiatives. In January 1973, students, townspeople, and faculty met to organize local and Washington demonstrations for Inauguration weekend, which included a Sandusky Street peace vigil and letter-writing campaigns [Source 1]. ![University chaplain James Leslie meeting with students and community members to discuss anti-war demonstrations.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1973-01-11/images/0001_Page%201_img2.webp)

Students also traveled to national anti-war marches, such as a major April 1971 Washington rally that drew 350,000 protesters [Source 4]. ![Anti-war demonstrators gathered on the Ellipse with a sign reading 'SMILE — ARMY INTELLIGENCE IS WATCHING'.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1971-04-29/images/0001_Page%201_img1.webp) Earlier campus demonstrations included protests against the speaking appearance of retired Air Force General Curtis B. LeMay in 1968, where students carried signs reading "Burn Draft Cards, Not Babies" [Source 3]. In April 1970, the OWU Peace Action Committee organized an "April Moratorium" featuring class boycotts and marches to protest war spending [Source 7]. Additionally, the OWU May Day Committee coordinated a People's Peace Concert and a Day of Conscience in May 1971 featuring activist films, faculty lectures, and memorial services [Source 6].

## ROTC and Draft Opposition

The military presence on campus became a focal point for student activism. In April 1970, 200 OWU students occupied the ROTC offices following the invasion of Cambodia [Source 5]. Years earlier, student leaders like Gordon Pettey moved in the Student Senate to abolish academic credit for Air Force ROTC [Source 5]. Despite these protests and tensions, a campus referendum conducted after the Kent State shootings revealed that 58 percent of students, faculty, and administrators favored retaining ROTC credit [Source 5]. Students also grappled with the military draft, as changing Selective Service policies threatened to make students with lower class standings eligible for induction [Source 9], while campus visitors like Yale Chaplain William Sloane Coffin, Jr. discussed draft resistance and public opposition to the war [Source 3, Source 8].

What was the OWU Student Senate's role in the 1969 ROTC debate?
Who was the OWU Peace Action Committee leader during the 1970 moratorium?

answer.text:
## Anti-War Actions in 1968

During 1968, anti-war actions covered by *The Transcript* were heavily characterized by direct campus confrontations, draft resistance, and protests against military and corporate recruiters. Students and activists engaged in both violent and non-violent demonstrations across the country [1968-01-31-28]. At Ohio Wesleyan University, visiting figures such as General Curtis B. LeMay were met with picketing students carrying signs with slogans like "Burn Draft Cards, Not Babies" [1968-01-31-28]. National anti-war efforts featured mass draft card turn-overs, including an event involving 1,000 students in Washington, as well as highway-blocking actions to stop buses carrying draftees to induction centers [1968-01-31-28]. Prominent figures like Yale Chaplain William S. Coffin and Dr. Benjamin Spock faced federal indictments for conspiring to counsel young men to resist the draft and collecting turned-in draft cards [1968-01-10-8]. Dr. Spock later visited OWU to speak as a war critic opening the L-M Series in Gray Chapel [1968-10-09-6]. Activists and academics like Howard Zinn publicly defended civil disobedience, arguing that legal channels were inadequate for halting the Vietnam war [1968-01-10-3].

![War critic Dr. Benjamin Spock speaking at a podium in Gray Chapel.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1968-10-09/images/0001_Page%201_img1.webp)
[1968-10-09-6]

## Anti-War Actions in 1970

By contrast, anti-war actions in 1970 evolved toward structured national moratoriums, economic protests, grassroots community organizing, and direct electoral politics. The Vietnam Moratorium Committee scheduled spring activities centered around "Tax Day" on April 15 to protest defense spending and highlight the economic dilemma caused by the war [1970-04-08-13, 1970-04-08-18]. OWU's Peace Action Committee planned student strikes, class boycotts, and local marches in Delaware alongside larger demonstrations in Columbus [1970-04-08-13]. Activists also undertook a three-day fast to demonstrate moral commitment, with the money saved distributed to victims of the Vietnam war and domestic poverty [1970-04-08-18]. Moving away from the earlier structure of adding one day of protest each month, the 1970 strategy emphasized locally oriented grassroots organizing, circulating "We Won't Go" statements where students refused armed services induction, and providing USO-type entertainment for overseas GIs [1970-04-08-18]. Furthermore, the peace movement integrated electoral politics by offering speakers bureaus, fund-raising, and media assistance to anti-war "dove" candidates running in the congressional elections [1970-04-08-18, 1970-01-14-8]. Business organizations such as Business Executives Move for Vietnam Peace also participated in moratoriums and rallied against the war due to spiraling inflation and economic costs [1970-01-28-20].

answer.text: ## Housing and Campus Life During the 1960s, housing and campus life for women at Ohio Wesleyan underwent notable shifts aimed at increasing social interaction. Coeducational residence patterns and coed dining halls were established to promote involvement between underclassmen [Source 4]. For instance, East-West Residence Hall accommodated both men and women, Thomson Hall became a women's dormitory, and Monnett Hall was closed as new housing became available [Source 4]. All campus dining units also became coeducational for the first time [Source 4]. ## Hours and Curfews Women's hours and curfews were strictly regulated by the Association of Women Students (AWS) and the university, sparking frequent student debates. In 1961, women students voted to return to a late minute policy that granted coeds 15 appealable late minutes without monitors [Source 7]. By 1968, hours were relaxed further: freshman women were permitted to stay out until 1:30 a.m. on weekends along with nine discretionary 1:30 permissions, sophomores received unlimited 1:30 a.m. hours, and juniors and seniors with parental consent could stay out until 5:30 a.m. any night [Source 1]. Proposals to change these restrictions, such as granting senior hours to students under 21 or implementing incentive-based hours, were frequently debated by student leaders, the AWS Executive Council, and Dean of Women Margaret Forsythe [Source 3, Source 8, Source 9]. ## Apartment Policies and Dress Codes University regulations strictly barred women from entering men's off-campus apartments, creating a widespread campus dilemma where rules clashed with student behavior [Source 2, Source 6, Source 10]. Although many students violated the policy or called for its elimination, administrators and student leaders debated whether the rules protected student morality or university public relations [Source 6, Source 10]. By 1968, AWS launched a formal study to explore more liberal visitation privileges in off-campus apartments [Source 2]. In addition to housing and hours, other aspects of daily life such as East Campus dress policies were subjects of continuous discussion between students and the administration regarding individual discretion [Source 5].

answer.text:
Ohio Wesleyan University's football team experienced varying levels of success across different seasons in the 1970s under head coach Jack Fouts.

## The 1970 and 1972 Seasons
During the 1970 season, the Bishops struggled to a 1-6 overall record and a 0-4 standing in the Ohio Conference, capped by a 35-0 loss to Wittenberg, though they did secure a 35-22 victory over Wabash [Source 4]. By the 1972 season, OWU showed early promise, improving to 2-1 after defeating Grove City College 41-6 behind a dominant rushing attack led by Jim Michals [Source 6, Source 7].

## The Mid-1970s Seasons
The 1973 squad finished the year with a 3-5-1 record [Source 8], suffering lopsided losses including a 41-7 defeat to Wittenberg and a 23-10 loss to Marietta [Source 9]. Later in the decade, the 1977 team finished 2-6 overall and winless in conference play at 0-4, a record largely attributed by Coach Fouts to an early injury to starting quarterback Phil Adkinson [Source 1]. The following year featured a very young lineup with numerous freshmen and sophomores [Source 3], leading into a season that concluded with a 3-5-1 record [Source 2].

answer.text:
## Overview of Campus Residence Halls

Ohio Wesleyan University featured several distinct residence halls, each with its own characteristics and amenities [Source 3]. Smith Hall was frequently the most requested dorm on campus, prized for offering private bathrooms and air conditioning [Source 3]. Welch Hall maintained an academic requirement of a 3.0 or higher grade point average for admission and provided students with its own computer lab, dining hall, workout room, multiple study rooms [Source 3], and kitchenettes equipped with microwaves following extensive renovations [Source 8].

## Social Atmosphere and Conditions

Thomson and Bashford Halls were known for having community bathrooms and vibrant, social atmospheres, which often made them popular with incoming freshmen [Source 3, Source 5]. Hayes Hall operated as the sole single-sex residence hall on campus with its own bathrooms [Source 3], though some students felt it restricted their social life and noted strict 24-hour quiet hours [Source 3, Source 7]. Stuyvesant Hall featured its own bathrooms [Source 3], but past student accounts described chaotic conditions during certain years, including heating failures, broken bottles on stair landings, and rowdiness [Source 7]. ![A portrait of Maryjane Miller accompanying her article.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1982-04-22/images/0004_Page%204_img2.webp) [Source 7] While some appreciated the historic or social aspects of the dorms, others criticized living spaces as being comparable to prison cells [Source 6].

## Housing Shortages and Adjustments

Due to enrollment fluctuations and housing squeezes over the years, Residential Life occasionally had to implement creative solutions to accommodate students [Source 2, Source 8, Source 9]. Basements in buildings like Stuyvesant Hall were renovated to create extra rooms [Source 2, Source 8], and temporary living arrangements such as triples, quads, or five-person units were sometimes utilized during years with higher enrollment [Source 2, Source 9]. An all-campus housing lottery system was also used to manage room assignments and allow seniors to move off-campus when housing was tight [Source 1, Source 2, Source 3].
